title_translit: Karmakandrahit Uda Vaishnav pragat karya, karma marag mukavi ananya marag Uda Vaishnavono pragat kidho te
title_en: How the Ritual-less Uda Vaishnavs Were Brought Forth — Renouncing the Path of Ritual Action, the Unique Path of the Uda Vaishnavs Was Revealed
translation:
Just as the kind of craftsman-guru one gets to prepare it determines whether the cloth turns out well- or poorly-woven.

In the Samagam, the Omkar (the primal sound) is called the ‘basto’ (the loom-warp cloth). This basto is the garment that binds one in bondage; thus the basto is the body the soul receives. The reckoning of one’s gotra (lineage) follows the tradition of the guru-forefathers one has received, and accordingly one’s ‘pot’ — that is, one’s inherent nature and qualities — is formed.

_Koi puje dev dera, koi puje bam. Jene jeva guru male, tene tevi gam._ (Some worship gods in temples, some worship Mahadev. As one gets a guru, so does one’s inclination become.) Some people worship gods and goddesses in temples, while others worship Mahadev (Shiva). Whatever kind of guru gives a person their teaching, that is the kind of devotional understanding they come to have.

_Ashvah shastram shastram vina vani narashcha nari cha, purushavisheshah prapta bhavantyayogyashcha yogyashcha ||119||_ (A horse, a weapon, a scripture, a veena, speech, man and woman — all become fit or unfit according to the particular person into whose hands they fall.) As stated in Mitrabheda [a section of the Panchatantra], a horse, a weapon, a scripture, a veena, speech, man and woman — all of these become fit or unfit depending on the kind of person into whose hands they fall.

HOW THE RITUAL-LESS UDA VAISHNAVS WERE BROUGHT FORTH — RENOUNCING THE PATH OF RITUAL ACTION, THE UNIQUE PATH OF THE UDA VAISHNAVS WAS REVEALED

Comparing the devotion of Kabirji and Narsinh Mehta from every angle, it has been shown that there is no difference between the two. (1) Both had the same guru — the gopis. (2) The dharma of both is the same — that of unique (ananya), one-pointed loving devotion. If anyone thinks that one of the two is higher and the other lower, it is said that such a person’s fortune is poor — there is no unlucky person worse than him. So from comparing the two, the conclusion reached is this: the enchanting flute-player, the Supreme Lord, is indeed the true God of this creation. In this world, this universe, whatever path of ritual action existed — recitation, austerity, vows and the like, sacrifices and offerings, the path of yoga, and devotion to the anadev (minor deities) — Jivanji had all of this given up, and he revealed the path that the unique Vaishnavs were to follow, the path of Satguru Namdev-Kabirji. Through this path, which particular practices of the path of ritual action were made to be given up, that has been shown. (3) The natural disposition (sahaj) of both is the same. (What is called the natural disposition of the gopis — Narsinh Mehta is just like the gopis, because he gave up his masculine identity; hence the natural disposition of the gopis is the same as the natural disposition of Narsinh Mehta.)

On this path, everyone was made a unique (ananya) Vaishnav in a single stroke. What was thereby prohibited from the path of ritual action is stated below.

1. No austerity (tap). 2. No pilgrimage (tirth). 3. No vows (vrat). 4. No yoga. 5. No sacrificial worship (yajan) — no keeping of vigils (jagaran). 6. No vow-offerings (manat) — that is, no keeping of vows of silence, no keeping of religious pledges, or tying a rakhi on the hand. 7. No offering of arghya (ritual water-offering). 8. No study or teaching of the Vedas. 9. No homa (fire-oblation). 10. No yagna (sacrifice). 11. No ritual action (karmakand). 12. Only the practice of devotion (bhakti) is to be done — not devotion to the anadev, but one-pointed, unique devotion alone. 13. Of the four things — tilak, tulsi, the Name of Ram, and the company of saints — one should gather only their essence, the finest part. As for the six systems of philosophy — Nyaya, Vaisheshik, Sankhya, Yoga, Purva Mimamsa (ritual action) and Uttara Mimamsa (Vedanta) — these are not to be pursued. 14. Marriage: without consulting any auspicious moment (muhurta), the bride and groom are to be married in a svayamvar, in the manner of Janak — that is, through the Prithvi Vivah (Earth-Wedding hymn).

In my commentary on the chapter of the Unique (Ananya) Devotee, I noted that this chapter falls roughly in the middle portion of the Samagam. In it, Jivanji Maharaj gave the clarification about Ramkabir’s Name of God, and that Name of God stands at the centre. Now comes the chapter about how the path of the Uda Vaishnavs was revealed as unique devotees — this chapter is like the heart of the Samagam. In it, one is to hold the above-mentioned 14 points inwardly with the oxygen — the life-breath — of Ramkabir, and through this oxygen, exhale out the carbon dioxide, the toxic breath, of the 14-point path of ritual action, so as to make one’s devotion pure and unblemished. Action (karma) exists in everyone, but the dharma of loving devotion (prem bhakti) is actionless (nishkarma). This Vishnu-devotion — the essence of essences, the finest of the finest in the universe — is what the Uda Vaishnavs have practised.

[Note on point 5, yajan: ‘yajan’ means having a sacrifice performed by others on one’s behalf, while ‘ijya’ means performing the sacrificial rites oneself.]

(Bhagavati Katha, Part 8, page 158, note on point 9, homa:) _Hom samast ved yagyamay hi hai. Sadharantaya yagya ka arth hai devatao ke liye dravya ka tyag karna. Ve yagya do prakar ke hote hain, yagya aur hom, jisme khade hokar havan karte hain aur antme vashatkar ka prayog hota hai, unki sangya yaag sangya hai, aur jinme baithkar havan kiya jata hai aur antme swaha ka prayog hota hai tatha jo yajya aur puronuvakya se rahit hote hain use hom kahte hain._ (Homa is entirely of the nature of Vedic sacrifice. Generally, ‘yajna’ means giving up material substance for the deities. Such sacrifices are of two kinds — yajna and homa. Those performed standing, ending with the utterance ‘vashat’, are called ‘yaag’; those performed sitting, ending with ‘swaha’, and lacking the yajya and puronuvakya formulas, are called ‘homa’.)

In ancient times there was a custom of holding a svayamvar. The bride’s relatives would invite all the kings for the svayamvar. When the kings arrived, the bride’s companions would describe the qualities of each one. Having seen and heard of their form and virtues, the bride would then place the wedding garland on the one she desired, after which the marriage would be performed with due rites. The svayamvars of Sita, Draupadi, Indumati and other such brides are illustrations of this. The custom of svayamvar existed ages ago, but Jivanji Maharaj conceived of a wedding practice of similarly excellent character and began an excellent tradition — marrying without consulting any auspicious moment — in a manner equal to the svayamvar. To have run the marriage tradition through the hymn of the Prithvi Vivah (Earth-Wedding), without Vedic ritual, is how great a revolution this is. The 14 prohibited points of the Uda Vaishnavs are Jivanji Maharaj’s forceful movement against anadev-worship and ritual action — and not only that, he had it put into practice in ordinary society, where it remains alive and unchanged to this day. The mention of the wedding canopy (sadhara mandap) is given in the Prithvi Dhol wedding hymn, and the hymn has been composed in such a way that the rite of marriage is performed while holding such excellent, meaning-filled, ideal thoughts. This shows Adhyaruji Maharaj’s devotion of feeling.

The practice of the muhurta was introduced later by the Brahmins. It is written in the Nigam Prakash that in ancient times people did not determine an auspicious moment for marriage, as is evident from the Ashvalayana and Baudhayana Sutras.

_Sarvakalam eke vivaham_ — Ashvalayana (Marriage may take place at any time.) _Sarvaprashasta vivahasya_ — Baudhayana (Every occasion is fit for marriage.)

_Surya-chandrau mangalash cha, budhash chapi Brihaspatih, shukrash cha shanish charo Rahuh, ketush cheti graha nava._ (Sun and Moon, Mars, Mercury, and also Jupiter, Venus and Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu — these are the nine planets.) Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rahu, and Ketu — these are the nine planets (grahas). Ketu is the comet, the ‘tailed star’.

_Narsinh naam bal bhajanko, tahe navgrah kya kare. Rahu Ketu Ravi Chandra, sada bhaktanke hetu. Sad sati na sanchare, buddhi anandko dani. Sada hot kalyan, kalyan kalyani. Vidhan haran mangal karan, Agradaske ur pad dhare. Narsinh naam bal bhajanko, tahe navgrah kya kare._ (By the strength of chanting the Name ‘Narsinh’, what can the nine planets do to him? Rahu, Ketu, the Sun, the Moon and the rest exist always for the good of the devotees. Not even the seven-and-a-half-year affliction [sadesati] touches him; the Name is the giver of right understanding and supreme bliss — it ever brings only well-being upon well-being. It removes obstacles and brings good fortune; Agradas holds its feet enshrined in his heart. By the strength of chanting the Name ‘Narsinh’, what can the nine planets do to him?) For practising devotion to God, the divine Name ‘Narsinh’ is exceedingly excellent. Whoever chants and worships taking this Name, the nine planets can do him no harm at all. Rahu, Ketu, the Sun, the Moon and the other planets are always working for the welfare of God’s devotees. Not even the sadesati — the seven-and-a-half-year affliction — can touch them. God, the giver of right understanding and supreme bliss, is always the well-wisher and benefactor of His devotees. Agradas holds in his heart the devotion of the God who removes the devotees’ obstacles and difficulties and who does good, auspicious things for them. How, then, could the nine planets ever afflict one who sings and chants this divine Name, Narsinh? They simply cannot.

Adhyaruji Maharaj too points to this divine Name ‘Narsinh’. This form of Narsinh is that in which God is the slayer of whoever torments His devotee.

_Parbrahm name mandal purawo, sumran Narsinh vir baulawo._ (Fill the sacred circle with the Name of the Supreme Brahm; invoke, through remembrance, the valiant Narsinh.) God assumes the form of Narsinh as a mighty, glorious manifestation. It further says,

_Shri Padmanabh Parbrahm em maliya, chhutya re sat lakh kod, chhutya re jantu prani avatarna e, ho Narhar, chhutya re._ (Thus we met Shri Padmanabh, the Supreme Brahm — released, O released, are hundreds of thousands and crores of births; released, O released, from taking birth as creatures and animals, O Narhar — released, O released.) The Supreme Brahm, as Lord Padmanabh, has now graced us in such a way that, by His manifestation, the sorrows of our hundreds of thousands and crores of births have ended, and taking birth in the bodies of the eighty-four lakh species of creatures and animals has come to an end. O Lord, having come now and met us as Lord Narsinh-Padmanabh, our hundreds of thousands and crores of births and rebirths have thus ceased.

Thus the Laghuras hymn has been composed giving importance to God’s Narsinh form, with ‘Narsinh’ as its refrain (dhruvpad). By the strength of the divine Name, the devotee does not fear the nine planets or afflictions such as the sadesati.

_Tulsi Raghubar dahena, sabai dahena tahe. Lagan muhurat shubh ghadi, Tulsi gane na kahe._ (Says Tulsi[das]: whoever has the Lord Raghubar’s right hand of favour upon him has everything favourable to him; Tulsi reckons no auspicious moment, hour, or occasion as necessary for him.) Tulsidas says that one upon whom God’s grace rests like His mighty right hand has, for that reason, the utmost grace of all the powers of the world. Hence such people, who live wholly by grace, hold no fear of the wheel of planets or the zodiac for marriage, nor of auspicious hours or moments; they pay no heed to muhurtas or the like for marriage. Devotees of God remain so intoxicated, so absorbed, in the rasa of loving devotion, that they take no account even of the most arrogant or powerful of people.

_Bhakt bawle gyani alhad, yogi bade nikhattu, karmakandi aise dole, jyon bhadeka tattu._ (Devotees appear mad, the wise appear carefree, great yogis appear useless and idle; ritualists roam about like a hired pack-horse.) Devotees remain absorbed in devotion; the wise are unconcerned with worldly things; yogis are useless, of no practical service; and ritualists go about restlessly, like a hired pack-animal — as if none of it truly concerns them, yet they are ever anxious, hasty, and thrashing about to perform and have others perform the rites of ritual action.

Kabir indeed lashed out at the pandits, saying: _Dharti angar na hata, ko pandit tha pas. Kaun muhurat thapiya, chand surya akas._ (When there was not even the earth, what pandit was there present? Who fixed the auspicious moment for creating the moon, the sun, and the sky?) Das Kabirji says: when there was nothing like the earth or the sky in this creation, which learned pandit was there beside God to indicate an auspicious hour, day, or moment for the creation of the moon, the sun, the sky, and so on?

In roughly the middle portion of the Samagam, the central subject for devotion to God is the divine Name — we have already examined at length the divine Name ‘Ram Kabir’. Now, to establish the loving devotion that is the very support of our life-breath — the unique (ananya) devotion to Vishnu — eighteen sakhis (couplets) and a kavit (poem) have been given.

Jivanji Maharaj prohibited the muhurta, and Adhyaruji too gave this his support. In the marriage rite, Adhyaruji has gone so far as to say that devotees even digest Time itself — that is, they swallow Time whole as a single morsel — and he has said that the planets, the gods, and the guardians of the directions (lokpals) too remain subordinate to God.

_Kal pachine kansar nipayo, santo pirse santo pirse arogo var-rai._ (Having digested Time, a sweet dish [kansar] has been prepared; the saints serve it, the saints serve it — partake of it, O bridegroom-king.) O Supreme Brahm, O Master, the saint-devotees have, through devotion, brought Time under their control and cooked it like the sweet kansar dish — they now serve it before You; partake of it. Through devotion practised over the span of life, they have turned Time to their advantage. These devotees are so fearless that they are not prepared to flatter even the planets, though it was God who created those very planets. Why should one who has taken refuge in the All-Powerful flatter the powerless? Hence they do not perform ritual acts such as ‘grah-shanti’ (planet-pacifying rites).

Here are the sakhis (couplets) concerning the chief Vishnu-devotion that has been enjoined to be practised in this universe.

_Ramanandi sampraday men, Uda Jivandas. Kul karma karani taji, kari Ramcharanki aas. ||1||_ (1. In the Ramanandi tradition comes Uda Jivandas: having forsaken the deeds and duties of family custom, he placed his hope in the feet of Ram.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: within the teaching-tradition established by Ramanandji, Jivandas set going the practice of the Uda devotee. Giving up the rites of family custom and Vedic custom prescribed by the bounds of lineage, he practised a devotion whose desire was only to go for refuge to the feet of God.

_Kabir ko kulmen ko panthmen, mitat na asha koi. Dono tyaj nyara rahai, bhagat kahave sai._ (Kabir says: some seek status in lineage, some in a sect — in neither does hope of true fulfilment end. He who gives up both and remains apart is the one truly called a devotee, O Lord.) Das Kabirji says: some people keep to the bounds of lineage, hoping to gain standing and honour in the world; some others hope to gain their standing within a sect or creed. But whoever gives up the craving for both lineage and sect, and practises devotion to God, is the one to be called a true devotee.

_Uda jaat Hanumanki, dini ekaj phal. Hari phal lino Jivana, te Sadguruke upgar. ||2||_ (2. The Uda devotees’ leap is of Hanuman’s kind — a single mighty leap; Jivan[das] has obtained the fruit of Hari through this — it is the favour of the Satguru.) Satguru Jivandasji Maharaj says: the character of the devotees of the Uda community is like that of Hanumanji. The Uda devotees too, like Hanumanji, made one single great leap and, crossing clean over ritual action and family custom, obtained at once the fruit that is the attainment of God — and this they obtained by the grace of the Satguru.

_Tirath vrat sab parhare, Uda tako naav. Kul karma tyaj Jivana, je samre Sitaram. ||3||_ (3. Whoever gives up all pilgrimage and vows is named ‘Uda’; Jivan[das says]: having forsaken family duty, such a one remembers Sitaram alone.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: those who give up pilgrimage, vows, and the like are known by the name of Uda devotees. Giving up family custom and ritual action, they remember only the divine Name Sitaram.

_Lok ved sab jaan de, jaav de dharti akash. Sadguru shabde raho Jivana, jahan prembhakti prakash. ||4||_ (4. Let go of all worldly and Vedic custom, let go even of earth and sky; Jivan[das says]: abide in the Word of the Satguru, wherein shines the light of loving devotion.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: give up the deeds of the lokik (Smarta — worldly custom, family custom) and the Vaidik (Shrauta — Vedic custom, ritual action, and the like), and let go even of the philosophical knowledge that dwells on the distinctions and mysteries of the five great elements — earth, sky, and the rest. Practise devotion to God only according to the teaching of the Satguru — for in that alone is experienced the light and joy of prem-lakshana bhakti (devotion characterised by pure love).

Revered Yadunath, in his Lintiyu no. 46, page 6, writes: ‘Earth, sky — when one lets go even of the order of origination of the five elements, how much more should one let go of worldly rites of worship and adoration.’

_Kabir sant soi janiye, rahe lokved ten door. Kaam krodh vyape nahi, soi sant bad shur._ (Kabir: know him alone to be a saint who stays far from worldly and Vedic custom; in whom lust and anger do not take hold — he alone is a truly great and valiant saint.) Das Kabirji says: only he is to be called a saint who remains apart from worldly custom and Vedic custom. Moreover, one in whom lust and anger do not arise — such a one is to be called a great, mighty, and valiant saint.

The Narad Bhakti Sutra, verse 8, says: _Nirodhastu lok-ved-vyapar-nyasah ||8||_ (Restraint, however, is the abandonment of worldly and Vedic activity.) It means: ‘restraint’ refers to giving up all Vedic — that is, all ritual — actions along with worldly activity. Once the picture of the world has faded from the mind, that devotion is no longer suited to perform any lokik (Smarta/worldly) or Vaidik (Shrauta/Vedic) action — it falls away entirely of its own accord.

_Uda kudha Jivana, jap tap tirath daan. Ved marag pichhe raho, jai malyo Harinaam. ||5||_ (5. Jivan[das] leapt clear over japa, tapa, pilgrimage, and charity; the path of the Vedas was left behind, and he attained the Name of Hari.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: the Uda devotees leapt clean over the practices of japa (recitation), tapa (austerity), pilgrimage, and charity; thereby the practices of the Vedic path were left behind, and the devotee became engaged in the remembrance of Hari.

_Nal vanar ne kalje, aise Harike daas. Bhav sagar dake Jivana, naam sharan vishwas. ||6||_ (6. Such, with the daring heart of the monkeys like Nal, are the servants of Hari; Jivan[das] leaps across the ocean of worldly existence, in faith upon the refuge of the Name.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: just as a wild monkey has the daring to leap from one tree to another, God’s devotees have that same daring, like Hanumanji’s; moreover, the devotees, keeping faith in devotion to the divine Name, leap across the ocean of worldly existence.

_Dalki tuki vanari, shabdhka chukya hans. Sabhaka chukya pandita, tinoka nirvansh._ (The female monkey who misses her leap from the branch, the swan who fails to heed the Word, and the pandit who fails in scriptural debate in the assembly — all three of these come to ruin.) The female monkey who, in leaping, fails to grasp the branch; the disciple who errs in following the guru’s teaching; and the learned pandit who errs in a scriptural debate in the assembly — all three of these are utterly destroyed.

_Udit dharam Uda tano, nahi Anadev prasang. Samran Sitaramko, vali sant sangati nihshank. ||7||_ (7. Risen is the dharma of the Uda devotee — no occasion at all for worship of the Anadev; only remembrance of Sitaram, and further, fearless company with the saints.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: the dharma of the Uda devotees stands at a high level, in which no occasion whatever could arise for devotion to the Anadev [minor deities]; moreover, these devotees, without any doubt or hesitation, practise the devotion of remembering Sitaram together in the company of the saints.

_Mido valyo Jivana, jo karu Anadevki sev. Sadguru sat tattva kahyo, je saache Raghupati dev. ||8||_ (8. Jivan[das] has sworn off ever serving the Anadev; the Satguru has told the true reality — that Raghupati [Ram] alone is the true God.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: he has renounced outright the matter of ever worshipping the Anadev again. He has told the Satguru the plain truth — that Ram alone is the true Supreme Being.

_Nav liti ab Jivana, jo karu aiso kaam. Sitapatiku tyajke, le Anadevko naam. ||9||_ (9. Jivan’s name is as good as erased, should he ever do such a deed — giving up Sitapati [Ram] and taking the name of the Anadev.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: if I should ever now give up devotion to Sitapati and take to worshipping the Anadev instead, then, utterly humbled, I would surrender myself entirely to You.

_Nak liti ab Jivana, jo karu aiso kaam. Mudadaku maati kare, chhaki Raghupati Rai. ||10||_ [unclear in parts] Jivandasji Maharaj says: if I should now worship the Anadev, then, utterly humbled, I would surrender myself entirely to You. Why should one, giving up devotion to King Ram, go and marry — and take as one’s master — something that has not even a trace of consciousness in it?

_To Anadev sir khasado, sevakke mukh laat. Ramnaam vin Jivana, jo bole duji vaat. ||11||_ (11. Then a shoe upon the head of the Anadev, and a kick to the mouth of his servant — says Jivan[das] — should anyone speak of anything other than the Name of Ram.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: now I shall utterly disregard the Anadev, and if any of his worshippers speaks of anything other than devotion to the Name of Ram, I shall confront and oppose him to his face.

_Ab aisi karu Jivana, duniyasu virodh. Anadevne anusare, taki kadhu khoj. ||12||_ (12. Now, says Jivan[das], I shall so oppose the world — I shall track down and expose whoever follows the Anadev.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: now I shall act so forcefully that I shall confront the improper, harmful practices current throughout the whole world, and I shall seek out and expose those who, though calling themselves Vaishnavs, are worshipping the Anadev.

_Mel mukat bhai Jivana, jab Sadguru diyo updesh. Sarag narak vaikunthlun, jyun daar upade kesh. ||13||_ (13. Jivan[das became] freed of every taint, when the Satguru gave him teaching; heaven, hell, and even Vaikunth were let go, as one plucks out a strand of hair by the root.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: when the Satguru gave his teaching, our deliverance came about. We came to understand the true reality of devotion, and so, just as one forcibly plucks out a hair from the head and casts it away, we removed even our expectations of heaven, hell, or Vaikunth.

_Narvasak je Jivana, Harijan taka naam. Sarag narak vaikunth taje, je samre Sitaram. ||14||_ (14. Jivan[das says]: he in whom no worldly craving remains — his name is ‘Harijan’, God’s devotee; he gives up heaven, hell, and Vaikunth, remembering Sitaram alone.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: one in whom no worldly desire or craving born of maya remains at all — such a one is called a devotee of God. Such devotees do not even wish to enjoy the pleasures of heaven, hell, or Vaikunth, but engage only in the remembrance and worship of the Name of Ram.

_Narayana-parah sarve na kutashchana bibhyati, svarga-apavarga-narakeshv api tulyaartha-darshinah._ (All those devoted to Narayana fear nothing from any quarter; they view heaven, liberation, and hell alike, with equanimity.) A devotee wholly devoted to Narayana, unattached and selfless, does not fear hell, nor desire heaven, nor even long for liberation.

_Chhati phate Jivana, nahi Ram bhagati aasan. Tuk tuk kaleja ho pade, to pave pad nirvan. ||15||_ (15. Jivan[das says]: devotion to Ram is no easy seat — the chest breaks open; only when the heart falls to pieces does one attain the state of liberation.) Jivandasji Maharaj says: to practise devotion to Lord Ram is no easy matter. When the inner being of one who practises this devotion becomes so overwhelmed by intense feeling that the heart is pierced through by its own anguish — when, from the suffering of the heart, the inner soul is so stirred that it seems to break into pieces — then one attains the bliss of God’s supreme abode.

_Kabir khari kasoti Ramki, khota take na koy. Ram kasoti te sahe, je jivat mrutak hoy. ||16||_ (16. Kabir: true is the touchstone-test of Ram — no counterfeit coin passes on it; only he endures the test of Ram who, while yet living, is as one dead.) Das Kabirji says: when God tests the true and the false devotee — if a devotee is selfish and proud, wavering the moment hardship comes, such a devotee will not be able to bear the test of devotion to God. Only that devotee who, like one already dead, is free of any kind of pride or self-interest will be able to bear the test of devotion to God — even when hardship comes, he will not give up his devotion.

Revered Yadunath Maharaj, in Lintiyu no. 56, on the back of page 15, writes: _Kabir kardi kasoti Ramki, khori tike na koy. Kaam kasoti so tike, jivat mutak hoy._ (Kabir: hard is the touchstone-test of Ram — nothing crooked stands the test upon it; that alone stands the test which, while living, becomes as one dead.) The meaning of this sakhi is explained thus: ‘living-dead’ is the name for one who, though alive, can die to the self — just as though you garland a person with flowers, he feels no joy from the honour of the garland; and though you strike a corpse five or twenty-five times, it feels no pain. In the same way, one who, though known to be alive, maintains this same kind of bearing, is said to be in the ‘living-dead’ state — and it is he alone who endures the test of Ram.

_Kabir Ram kaho to mari kaho, jivat bahu na Ram. Jab lag jivat Ram hai, tab lag kacha kaam._ (Kabir: if you would say ‘Ram’, say it as one dying; while alive, do not much claim to have Ram — as long as one merely calls upon Ram while still living in the ego, so long the work of devotion remains unripe.) If one wishes to take the Name of Ram, one should take it without pride, in humility, and free of any desire. If you hold on to selfish desire and pride, God Ram’s grace will not increase for you. As long as you take the Name of Ram while still holding on to ego and attachment, your practice remains incomplete.

_Kabir mohi maraneka chav hai, maru to Ram darbar. Kabahuk deen dayalke, koi das muva darbar. ||2||_ (Kabir: I have a longing to die — but let me die in the court of Ram; then perhaps the compassionate one, merciful to the humble, will feel that some servant has died at his court.) I have a great desire to die — but I ask that I may die only in the court of Ram. Perhaps then it will seem, even to the gracious Lord, that some devotee has fallen in service for the sake of Ram.

_Milna to dil kholke, ladhna to shir phodke. Bhakti duheli Ramki, nahi kayarka kaam. Nisnehi nirghar ko, aatho prahar sangram._ (To meet God, meet with an open heart; to fight, fight breaking one’s own head. Devotion to Ram is hard — it is no work for a coward; for one who is loveless and without resolve, it is a battle through all eight watches of day and night.) Devotion to Lord Ram is very hard and difficult — it is no task for the fearful or the faint-hearted. For it, one who is entirely free of any kind of desire has to struggle unceasingly, confronting it constantly.

As to how difficult devotion to Ram is, Kabir has given a whole section (ang) on devotion concerning it.

_Kabir vipat bhali Harinaam let, kaya kasoti dukh. Ram naam bin kis kamki, maya sampat sukh._ (Kabir: adversity is good if it comes while taking the Name of Hari — even the body’s trial and pain; without the Name of Ram, of what use are the pleasures of worldly wealth and prosperity?) Das Kabirji says: however much hardship comes in the taking of the divine Name, it is still good and beneficial — even if the body must pass through trial, there is no harm in that. But without the Name of Ram, of what use is the wealth of worldly pleasures and enjoyments?

_Nanak Nana parakhu, chale chauta mahen. Khotko khota kahai, vaki nanda nahen._ (Nanak and Nana, the assayers, go about in the open marketplace; they call a false coin false — in that there is no fault of theirs.) Nanak says: assayers, who test currency coins, move about in the open marketplace, in the public square, and when they call a false coin false, they are not to be blamed for it.

_Jyun soni sona kasai, sab mal kadhe shodh. Gyani guru aise kasai, sab karma kadhe bodh._ (As a goldsmith assays gold and, examining it, removes all its impurity, so does the wise guru assay the disciple and, through understanding, remove all his karmic bonds.) Gyaniji Maharaj says: just as goldsmiths properly assay gold, examine it, and purify it by removing the mixed-in impurity and dross found in it, so too does the guru, in that same way, properly examine the disciple, remove his bonds of karma, and give him the teaching of devotion.

_Kach kathir adhir nar, kasa na upaje prem. Parasram kasani sahai, kai hira ke hem._ (Glass, base-alloy metal, and a restless man — when tested, love does not arise in them; Parashuram says: only a diamond or gold can bear the assay.) Parashuram says: glass, base metal (zinc alloyed with tin and lead), and a restless, impatient person do not succeed in the trial of love. Only a diamond or gold can endure such a trial.

_Kabir hansa bagla ek rang, maan sarovar jay. O bag dhundhe magh machhli, o hans mukta phal khaya._ (Kabir: the swan and the crane are one in colour, and both go to Man Sarovar; but the crane searches there for reeking fish, while the swan feeds on pearls.) Das Kabirji says: the swan and the crane are the same in colour, and if both go to Man Sarovar, this crane will search out from it the fish reeking of its smell, while this swan will feed on pearls.

Kavit — _Chugat hans nij naam, tahan bag karma kit na bhave. Khir nir niravar kare, so nad hans kahave. Bag machhi chug khaye, bag na mugta phal chug jane. Karat hanski hod, gat apni na pahichane. Maan sarovar hans ghar, bag chhilar sarbhar kare. Parasram jan hanski, kaha baglo sarbhar kare._ (The true swan pecks and feeds on its own proper food; there, the crane’s habit of feeding on worms does not suit it. That one who separates milk from water is called the true swan. The crane pecks and eats fish; the crane does not know how to peck at pearls. It vies in competition with the swan, yet does not recognise its own inferior state. Man Sarovar is the swan’s home; the crane makes do with a shallow puddle. Parashuram says: how could a crane ever compare with the true swan?) Parashuram says: the swan, true to its renown, feeds on pearls; and such a swan does not care for the work the crane does, of eating worms and fish. It is called the great swan because it separates milk from water. The crane, for its part, eats fish with its beak; the crane does not know how to pick up grains of pearl with its beak, yet still it tries to enter into competition with the swan, without recognising what its own conduct and understanding are really like. Man Sarovar is the swan’s dwelling place, whereas the crane keeps close company with ponds and puddles. Parashuram says: how could a crane ever properly be compared with swan-like people?

_Swang ek boho antra, koyal kagda joy. Pativrata aur punsali, bhelan bane na doy._ (The outward form is one, but the inward difference is great — see the koel and the crow; a chaste wife and an unchaste woman — the two can never become alike.) Nana Parekh says: the koel [cuckoo] and the crow are alike in their black colour and outward form, but there is a great difference in their qualities. A chaste, devoted wife and an unchaste woman — these two can never be alike in their qualities.

_Swang ek boho antra, jyo bagla aur hans. Ek bhekh pade bhramme, ek kate Kalko kans._ (The outward form is one, but the inward difference is great, as with the crane and the swan; one, in that guise, falls into delusion, the other cuts through the snare of Death.) Nana Parekh says: just as the crane and the swan are alike in colour and appearance, there is a great difference in their qualities. One, of the crane’s kind, falls into the delusion of maya, while the other, of the wise and understanding swan’s kind, cuts through the bonds of death (Kal).

_Kabir hariya jane rukhda, pani tana sneh. Suka kashth na pallave, jo keta uthe meh. ||2||_ (Kabir: it is the green tree that knows the love of water; dry wood does not sprout leaves, no matter how much rain may fall.) Das Kabirji says: it is green, living trees that know love with water; but on dry wood, however much rain falls, it has no effect whatsoever.

The devoted followers who compiled the Samagam have, in keeping with this occasion, included the following hymn.

(Raag Sarang.) _Chalo hansa desh sohamane (hansa), chalo desh sohamane. Yah sansar osko pani (moti), kirne chhute nahi pavano. ||tek|| Kaha Brahmalok kaha Shivlok, kaha Vishnulok thaharavano. Chalo hansa ve desh amar hai, jahan thai phir na avano. ||hansa||1|| Shunyakaal aur jot swarupi, e lokan man bhavano. Yoni sankashta mite nahi kabahu, bhram bhatki phir avano. ||hans||2|| Hansa hoy so va desh jai hai, kahat Kabir samjhavano. Jahan nahi Ram thagori aave, janam maran nahi dahano. ||hansa||3||_ (Come, O swan, to the beautiful land — come to that beautiful land. This world is but dewdrop water taken for pearl — its shine can never truly be attained. What is Brahmalok, what is Shivlok, what is Vishnulok, that one should settle there? Come, O swan, to that land which is deathless — whence, once there, one never has to return. Even the realm of the Void and of light-form is only a place dear to certain minds; the affliction of the womb is never removed there — one strays in delusion and comes back again. Only a true swan goes to that supreme land — thus Kabir explains it — where the deceit of maya never comes, and there is no more burning pain of birth and death.) O supreme devotee, let us go to that excellent abode. This world is as insubstantial as dewdrop water that only appears like a pearl — it is that false and fleeting. From the water of this dew, which merely looks like a pearl, we can never obtain the true lustre of a real pearl. So too, whether it be Brahmalok, Shivlok, or Vishnulok, all these realms are subject to destruction — of what use, then, is it to dwell there? But, O devotee soul, there is a land, an abode, that is deathless, from which, once there, one never has to return again to birth and death. Going into the false-time creation of the three-natured world of Omkar-light is the land dear to the worshippers of the Anadev. For such people, the suffering of coming and going through the womb never ceases — they wander round and round through such realms and come back again into this world. But it is the excellent devotee alone who goes to such a supreme abode — thus does Kabirji explain — a place where there is none of the deceiving maya fashioned by God, so that the pain of birth and death need never be borne.

The compilers of the Samagam have further included two more hymns in the Samagam.

(Raag Sarang.) _Hansa hans mile sukh hoi, jahan sahaj samagam hoi. ||tek|| Khat darshan pakhand chhanuva, bhekh banave loi. Char varan aur ved kateba, hans unthe nyara hoi. ||1|| Hansa to hai premka pyasa, sau vaikunth na hoi. Jahan mukat sakal mamtaki, hans taje jaise chhoi. ||2|| Hansa hamara shabad basera, shabad ahari hoi. So hansa sat lok pahucha, tahan jamra rahya roi. ||3|| So jamra jaay teen lok par, bandhe antariksh joi. Tahi chhod chale shabad hamara, tako aava-gavan na hoi. ||4|| Kahat Kabir pratit kijiye, hans na rahat bachhoi. Lei basavu me deev sagamag, hanse hans samoi. ||5||_ (When swan meets swan there is joy — where there is a natural, effortless coming-together. The six philosophical systems and the ninety-six sects put on their various guises. From the four varnas and from the Vedas and the scriptures of other faiths alike, the true swan stands apart. The swan is thirsty only for love — a hundred Vaikunths could not satisfy it. Where there is liberation from all attachment, the swan drops it just as one sheds a covering. Our swan’s dwelling is the Word; it feeds only on the Word. Such a swan reaches the True Abode, where even Yama is left weeping, unable to follow. Yama can go over the three worlds and bind beings even in the reaches of the sky; but our Word travels beyond even that, and for it there is no more coming and going. Kabir says: have faith in this — the true swan does not remain separated; I shall settle it upon the lamp aglow, where swan merges into swan.) When one saint-devotee meets another saint-devotee, there is great joy — where such a meeting occurs, a natural coming-together happens of its own accord, and an intense loving union takes place. People, following the six systems of philosophy and the ninety-six varieties of hypocrisy, put on various outward guises. Saint-devotees stand apart from the four varnas and from the Vedas and other scriptures alike. These saintly souls are eager only for love-natured devotion; such saintly souls are not to be found in Vaikunth, for they have no desire even for Vaikunth. In that state, they are untouched by any attachment or possessiveness — such saints are free of all these attachments, and they cast off possessiveness the way one casts off something untouchable. Our saints are ones who live according to the teaching of the Satguru — their eating, movement, that is, all their daily activity, is carried out according to that teaching. Such saintly souls reach the True Abode, the supreme realm, where even Yamaraj cannot go, and so he is left to lament. This Yamaraj can go into all three worlds and can even move through the paths of the sky; but those who, abandoning that three-world universe, live according to my teaching go beyond even him, to where they never again have to come back and move about in this world of death. Kabirji says that such saintly living souls never remain parted from this abode. I shall bring them and settle them in the most excellent, radiant, supreme abode, where these saints will be united together with the other saints. And further, Nana Parekh’s hymn too has been presented here.

(Raag Sarang.) _Harijan hans sulakshana santo, Harijan hans sulakshana. Nishadin preet nibhaye jaye, chhande nahi pan apna. ||tek|| Maan sarovar tachake vasi, aan sarovar avagana. Vake sant sangat hai pyari, salilsangsu risana. ||1|| Muhta phal bina chanch na bahe, karam kit nahi chakhana. Vake bade bade bhupati chahe, khit nitke parakhana. Vadgunthe nirgun kare nyara, Parbrahmke pyara dhana. ||3|| Bhayeg phale jo male jan aisa, prem bhagat paripurana. Nano kahe bali jau taki, pal pal leu ovarana. ||4||_ (The Harijan is of the swan’s fine character, O saints — the Harijan is of the swan’s fine character. Day and night he keeps love, never abandoning his own vow. He dwells at the shore of Man Sarovar; he disdains any other lake. To him the company of saints is dear; he is displeased with the company of mere water. Unless it is a pearl, his beak does not open — he does not taste the worms of ordinary deeds. Even great kings desire him; distinguishing pure from impure is his skill. Being of the great quality, he sets himself apart from what is qualityless; he is dearly beloved of the Supreme Brahm. Blessed and fruitful is he who meets such a person, one full and complete in loving devotion. Nano [Nana Parekh] says: I offer myself to him, and moment by moment I would wave an offering over him.) God’s devotees (Harijans) possess fine good qualities. O saints, the Harijans possess fine good qualities. They always uphold their loving devotion, and they never let go of their vow. They are like the swans that dwell at the shore of Man Sarovar — high souls who dwell at the shore of unique devotion. For them, other lakes and ponds — that is, devotion to the Anadev — hold no attraction beside the pure devotion that is like Man Sarovar. Only the company of saints is dear to them; they are displeased at keeping company with mere worldly water. Just as swans do not put their beaks into fish and the like, but only into pearls, in the same way these saints do not so much as taste the fish, so to speak, of ritual action — they do not accept ritual action at all — apart from the pearl that is the divine Name. Nothing besides the divine Name tastes sweet to them, or is pleasing to them. Therefore they do only the worship of the divine Name. Even the greatest of great men wish to love such excellent Harijans, who, like this swan, separate the water of maya from the milk of the Supreme Brahm. These Harijans are such as render themselves free of the three gunas (qualities of nature); they are thus the Lord’s most beloved devotees. If our good fortune should come to fruition, we too might obtain such Harijans, in whom there is complete and perfect love-natured devotion. Nana Parekh says: I am utterly devoted to such Harijans, and moment by moment I wish them well.

_Jage jad so jivani, mui na jage koy. Gyani sukha yon rah gaya, jivat hariya hoy._ (What sprouts though inert is truly alive; nothing dead ever sprouts again. Gyani[ji says]: it remains dry as it was, but what is truly living turns green.) Gyaniji Maharaj says: that whose roots sprout when given water is alive; but that which has died and dried up does not sprout. What has dry roots remains just as it is, unchanged, but what is living turns green with new growth.

_Kabir bhavatake bichhuda, dagh pare dil bich. Sukha kabdu na pallave, jo saat samudran sinch._ (Kabir: one parted from his beloved bears a burn-mark within his heart; dry wood never sprouts leaves, even if you were to water it with the seven seas.) Das Kabirji says: one who has been separated from his beloved bears a scar upon his heart; just as dry wood, however much you water it — even with as much water as the seven seas — never sprouts, so too does the lover’s heart remain wounded.

The Uda Vaishnavs are free of ritual action; they possess, like the swan, the art of separating water from milk — such Vaishnavs are said to separate maya from Brahm. This Samagam took place at Shahpura, where the code of this Uda dharma was set forth. This tradition of the Uda Vaishnavs is that of unique (ananya) devotion to Vishnu. What such unique conduct looks like, Kabirji has written a whole ‘ang’ (section) about.

THE SECTION ON THE UNIQUE (ANANYA) DEVOTEE

_Kabir kul adhar aur tan adhar, adhar vidya aur daam. E adhar taji nishchal rahe, sau pave agochar gam. ||1||_ (Kabir: support in one’s lineage, support in one’s body, support in learning, and support in wealth — one who abandons these supports and remains unshaken attains the unreachable, imperceptible state.) Das Kabirji says: those who consider themselves great because of a high lineage, or think their own body excellent — such bodily pride — or those who consider themselves great because of their learning or their wealth and possessions — whoever gives up all such kinds of pride and remains free of them can attain the supreme state.
